# Benchmarking and Performance Engineering {#sec-benchmarking}

::: {.callout-note title="Status: complete first draft"}
:::

A streaming engine that produces correct answers slowly is, for
most workloads, useless. NebulaStream cares about performance
deeply enough to track it continuously, expose it through a public
dashboard, and run a dedicated instrumentation build alongside the
debug and release builds.

This chapter walks through how the engine is benchmarked, what
infrastructure exists, and which performance gotchas are worth
knowing.

---

## 21.1 Conbench: continuous benchmarking {#sec-conbench}

The README points at a Conbench instance at
`bench.nebula.stream/c-benchmarks/`. Conbench [@conbench] is a
benchmarking framework that runs the engine's benchmark suite on
every commit and tracks results over time. The dashboard shows:

- Per-benchmark throughput and latency graphs across commits.
- Regression detection (a commit that slows a benchmark by more
  than a configurable threshold flags up).
- Per-architecture breakdowns (x86_64, ARM).

This is the engine's primary tool for catching performance
regressions. A bug that drops join throughput by 20% will show
on the Conbench graph before it shows in any user complaint.

---

## 21.2 The benchmark suite {#sec-benchmark-suite}

Two locations:

- **Microbenchmarks.** `nes-common/benchmarks/` for component-
  level tight loops. Things like the `ExceptionBenchmark.cpp`
  that measures the cost of throwing/catching an exception.
- **Macrobenchmarks.** `nes-systests/benchmark/` and
  `nes-systests/benchmark_small/` for full end-to-end query
  benchmarks. These reuse the systest format from Chapter 20 with
  one difference: the expected-output section is replaced with
  a throughput target and the test is judged on time-to-complete
  rather than correctness alone.

The macrobenchmark suite includes recognisable industry workloads:

- **Yahoo Streaming Benchmark.** Aggregation over a stream of
  ad-impression events. The classic benchmark for streaming
  engines.
- **Linear Road.** Spatial-temporal event processing across road
  segments. From the original Aurora paper.
- **Manufacturing.** Industrial IoT scenario; per-machine and
  per-product event aggregation.

Each benchmark has a small variant (in `benchmark_small/`) that
runs in CI on every commit, and a full variant that runs nightly.

---

## 21.3 The instrumentation build {#sec-instrumentation-build}

The repository has four build directories that each correspond
to a build type:

- `cmake-build-debug` — debug build with full assertions and
  TRACE logging.
- `cmake-build-release` — release build with -O3 and ERROR
  logging.
- `cmake-build-docker` — release build inside the Docker dev
  image.
- `cmake-build-instrumentation` — a special build with
  performance instrumentation enabled.

The instrumentation build is the one the team uses for serious
performance work. It enables:

- Per-buffer latency instrumentation (the four-point latency
  measurement mentioned in the engine's recent commit messages).
- Detailed per-operator and per-pipeline statistics.
- Profiler-friendly symbols (frame pointers, no aggressive
  inlining).

Instrumentation builds are slower than release but expose the
data needed for performance analysis. The CI does not run them on
every commit; they are typically used on dedicated hardware for
specific benchmarking sessions.

---

## 21.4 The sanitizer matrix {#sec-sanitizer-matrix}

Performance work and correctness work intersect in the sanitizer
matrix. The CI matrix in CLAUDE.md describes:

> x86_64/arm64 × libcxx/libstdcxx × Debug/RelWithDebInfo/Release ×
> address/undefined/thread/none sanitizers + clang-tidy diff +
> code coverage.

Each axis multiplies the build cost. The full matrix is large and
runs nightly; subsets run on every PR.

**ASan** (address sanitizer) catches buffer overruns, use-
after-frees, and memory leaks. NebulaStream's reference-counted
buffer pool means leaks are rare, but ASan still catches edge
cases.

**TSan** (thread sanitizer) catches data races. The two-queue
scheduler (Chapter 15) and the lock-free hash maps (Chapter 16)
get the most use of TSan. Streaming engines are concurrent by
nature; TSan catches what locks miss.

**UBSan** (undefined behaviour sanitizer) catches signed integer
overflow, null-pointer dereferences, alignment violations.
Important for any C++ codebase, especially one with hot paths
written in raw arithmetic.

These do not run in production builds — sanitizers add
substantial overhead — but they catch enough bugs in CI that
keeping them in the matrix pays for itself many times over.

---

## 21.5 Performance gotchas worth knowing {#sec-performance-gotchas}

A handful of subtleties show up repeatedly in NebulaStream
performance work.

**INTERPRETER mode is 10-100× slower than COMPILER.** Mentioned
in earlier chapters but worth reiterating: do not benchmark
INTERPRETER mode unless you are studying the interpreter
specifically.

**Buffer-pool sizing matters.** A pool that is too small backpressures
sources and limits throughput. A pool that is too large wastes
memory the engine could be using for hash maps. The default 1024
buffers is a reasonable starting point; the right value for
production workloads depends on operator concurrency.

**Logging is expensive.** TRACE-level logging on a hot path costs
thousands of cycles per record. Benchmarking with TRACE is
benchmarking the logger, not the engine. Use Release or
Benchmark builds, not Debug, for performance numbers.

**Sanitizers slow things down a lot.** TSan can be 5-10× slower
than a clean build. Do not be alarmed if a sanitizer-equipped
benchmark shows numbers very different from a release benchmark;
they are measuring different things.

**The format-conversion bottleneck.** For some workloads (CSV-
heavy ingestion), the engine's hot path is in the input
formatter, not the operators. Profilers should focus there
first.

::: {.callout-tip title="Real-system reference: Flink's benchmarking"}
Apache Flink runs its own continuous benchmarking
infrastructure ([flink.apache.org/benchmarks](https://flink.apache.org/benchmarks/)).
Looking at Flink's numbers next to NebulaStream's is
instructive — Flink, being a JVM engine running in the cloud, is
optimised for sustained throughput on a stable cluster;
NebulaStream is optimised for low latency in heterogeneous
deployments. The benchmarks each system runs reflect those
priorities. A horse-race comparison would be misleading; a
side-by-side comparison of *which workloads each engine is
strong on* would be illuminating.
:::

## 21.6 What to measure when starting work {#sec-what-to-measure}

For someone about to do performance work on NebulaStream:

1. **Run the relevant benchmark first.** Establish a baseline. If
   you change `nes-query-engine/`, run the join benchmark before
   and after.

2. **Use the Chrome trace.** Enable
   `GoogleEventTracePrinter` (Chapter 17) and visualise. The
   trace will show you exactly which operators are taking time
   and which are idle.

3. **Profile with `perf` or Instruments.** A flame graph on the
   instrumentation build shows where cycles go. Most hot-path
   surprises live here.

4. **Compare modes.** If COMPILER is slow, INTERPRETER will tell
   you whether the slowness is in operator logic or in the JIT.

5. **Compare commits.** Conbench gives you a per-commit baseline.
   Did your change regress a benchmark? Conbench will tell you.

The engine has invested visibly in these tools. Use them.

---

## Summary {#sec-ch21-summary}

NebulaStream's performance engineering rests on continuous
benchmarking via Conbench, a multi-build matrix that includes
debug, release, and instrumentation builds, and a CI sanitizer
matrix that runs ASan, TSan, and UBSan across architectures and
libcxx flavours. The benchmark suite includes industry-standard
workloads (Yahoo Streaming, Linear Road) plus engine-specific
microbenchmarks. Common performance gotchas — INTERPRETER mode
overhead, logging cost, sanitizer slowdowns, format-conversion
bottlenecks — are catalogued for the practitioner. The Chrome
trace and per-buffer instrumentation are the engine's primary
visualisation tools.

---

## Reading exercises {#sec-ch21-exercises}

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 21.1: open Conbench"}
Visit `https://bench.nebula.stream/c-benchmarks/`. Look at one
benchmark's history graph over the last 100 commits. Do you see
any regressions? Any improvements? What changed?
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 21.2: build instrumentation"}
Configure and build with the instrumentation flag enabled (look
for the relevant CMake option in the build directory layout).
Run a join benchmark. How much slower is it than the release
build? What additional output does it produce?
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 21.3: TSan a lock-free path"}
Build with `-DNES_USE_SANITIZER=thread` and run the
`TaskQueueTest` from Chapter 15. TSan will instrument the
folly queues and the semaphore. Are there any reported races?
There should be none — but if there were, TSan is exactly the
tool that would catch them.
:::
